The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p99 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-12T14:22:00Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-12T14:22:02Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-12T14:16:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-12T14:22:19Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 6 minutes 19 seconds {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 3 minutes 5 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-12T14:25:08Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 1.6% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 2.5% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none beyond its normal variation - no more than two of the steps the rate moves in.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p99 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 198.86666666666667 ms {series_before} before it began, 1395.6666666666667 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 2081 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-11-12T14:22:02Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighLatency on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-11-12T14:22:04Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-11-12T14:22:04Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-11-12T14:22:05Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 14:22 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-12T14:22:05Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 361 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-12T14:22:05Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 14:16 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-12T14:22:05Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-12T14:22:10Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys and releases, and flag changes from the flag provider's history, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 12 14:17 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-12T14:22:10Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 1 {T9.2} production change
  - [T10] 2026-11-12T14:22:10Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read the service register - the service calls io-pricing (internal, owned by checkout-platform), io-summary-cache (internal, owned by checkout-platform), io-pay (third-party, owned by IO Payments Ltd)
  - [T11] 2026-11-12T14:22:10Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 36 {T11.2} minutes before 14:22 {T11.3}
  - [T12] 2026-11-12T14:22:10Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 130 {T12.2} log lines
  - [T13] 2026-11-12T14:22:17Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T13.2} candidate cause, best first: C1
  - [T14] 2026-11-12T14:22:17Z {T14.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T15] 2026-11-12T14:22:18Z {T15.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 1 {T15.2} flag change by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T15.3} hour before 14:22:17 {T15.4}
  - [T16] 2026-11-12T14:22:18Z {T16.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
  - [T17] 2026-11-12T14:22:18Z {T17.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T18] 2026-11-12T14:22:19Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for C1, moved from ON to OFF
  - [T19] 2026-11-12T14:22:19Z {T19.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 14:23 {T19.2} - up to 220s {T19.3}
  - [T20] 2026-11-12T14:25:08Z {T20.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 14:22 {T20.2}
  - [T21] 2026-11-12T14:25:08Z {T21.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T22] 2026-11-12T14:25:08Z {T22.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - set flag [typical-purchase-feature] OFF and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T23] 2026-11-12T14:26:07Z {T23.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/573

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-11-12T14:15:47Z {P1.1} flag-toggle typical-purchase-feature by admin: feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched on
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [Ga6f5] INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off - 200 {Ga6f5.1} evaluations - 29 {Ga6f5.2} occurrences in 29 {Ga6f5.3} minutes, 13:46–14:14 {Ga6f5.4}
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 56 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 36 {G46bc.2} minutes, 13:46–14:21 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 35 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 36 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 13:46–14:21 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.4} to 2.50% {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.00% {Gbac1.6}, highest at 14:02 {Gbac1.7}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 2 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 26 {Gad41.2} minutes, 13:57–14:22 {Gad41.3}
  - [Gc8c4] INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off 163 {Gc8c4.1} / on 37 {Gc8c4.2} - 200 {Gc8c4.3} evaluations - 1 {Gc8c4.4} occurrence in 1 {Gc8c4.5} minute, 14:15 {Gc8c4.6}
  - [Gd44a] INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=on - 200 {Gd44a.1} evaluations - 7 {Gd44a.2} occurrences in 7 {Gd44a.3} minutes, 14:16–14:22 {Gd44a.4}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] Feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched on at 2026-11-12T14:15:47Z {C1.1}. p99 latency jumped from about 200ms {C1.2} to 1000-2000ms {C1.3} from 2026-11-12T14:16:00Z {C1.4}, while p50, p95, error rate, memory and CPU stayed at baseline. No deploy occurred, the rollout and pods were unchanged, and the dependencies show no failure. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.88 {C1.5}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for [C1] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault: `typical_spend_per_item` in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py found the middle price by calling `remaining.remove(min(remaining))` `(n-1)//2` times. Each `min` and each `remove` is a full pass over the list, so a history of n purchases costs about n² comparisons. Most histories are short, so the cost lands only on shoppers with long ones. That matches the investigation: p99 jumped while p50 and p95 stayed at baseline once `typical-purchase-feature` sent requests down this path (`render_spend_summary` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py calls it when `use_typical_spend` is set). The flag only exposed the fault; the function itself is the fault.
      
      The fix sorts the prices once and returns the element at index `(n-1)//2`. That is the same lower-of-two-middles element the old loop returned (repeated prices still count once per purchase), and it costs O(n log n). An empty history still raises ValueError, as `min([])` did before, so callers see no change in what is raised. The signature and return value are unchanged, so `render_spend_summary` and the account page need no change.
      
      The test: tests/io_shop/test_typical_spend.py keeps every existing correctness case. It adds a case that counts comparisons on a 2,001-purchase history, using an int subclass whose `__lt__` increments a counter, and asserts the count stays under 30 {F1.1} per purchase. The old repeated-min loop does roughly 1.5 {F1.2} million comparisons on that input, far over the bound. A single sort does a few tens of thousands, within it. The test also checks that the returned middle is still correct. Counting comparisons rather than timing keeps the test independent of how fast the machine is.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus:
  - [U1] typical_spend_per_item at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:67, in render_spend_summary: calls it: return typical_spend_per_item(account)
  - Where [F1] says otherwise of these lines, they stand.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #573 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P1].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: With typical-purchase-feature on, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item (src/io_shop/typical_spend.py). That function finds the middle price by removing the smallest remaining price over and over until it reaches the middle, and each min and each remove is a full pass over the list. Its work therefore grows far faster than the length of a shopper's purchase history, so requests for shoppers with long histories became very slow while requests for most shoppers stayed fast. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a new shop feature sent shoppers' pages through a calculation of their typical spend that likely does far more work the more purchases a shopper has made, so pages for shoppers with long purchase histories became very slow.
still_at_risk: If typical-purchase-feature is switched back on before a fix is in place, the slowest shop requests could slow down again in the same way.
symptom: The slowest shop page loads slowed sharply for some shoppers
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' slowest requests took much longer to load. The alert fired on the slowest tail of request durations across the service's replicas, and the Investigator placed the start at the onset. Failed requests did not rise: the account page error rate stayed within its usual range and peaked before the onset. (cites AL1; T6, under "What Argus did, in order"; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: Requests began running the code path behind typical-purchase-feature. Admin switched the flag on at {P1.1}. Before that, every flag evaluation logged came back off. In the minute of the switch the evaluations were mixed, and from the onset on, every evaluation logged came back on. (cites P1, under "Changes to production it read"; Ga6f5, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gc8c4, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gd44a, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2 ruled_out 2: Any other flag change: the flag provider's history for the hour before showed no flag change by anyone but Argus other than this one. (cites T15, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3: With the flag on, the account page's spend summary calls a typical-spend calculation whose work, by Code-Fix's reading, grows far faster than the length of a shopper's purchase history, so shoppers with long histories waited much longer. (cites U1, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus"; F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
contributing_factors 1: The flag went straight from off for every evaluation to on for every evaluation. No staged rollout to a small share of shoppers was seen, and no automatic guard that turns a just-changed flag off when latency rises was seen.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: A staged rollout would have exposed only a few shoppers to the slow path, and a latency guard could have turned the flag off without waiting for the alert and an agent's action.
contributing_factors 2: No test or check of how the flagged code path performs with long purchase histories was seen before the flag was switched on in production.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: A test with a long purchase history would likely have shown the slow calculation before the flag was turned on, so the slow path would not have reached shoppers.
action_items 1: Roll out io-shop feature flag changes to a small share of traffic first, rather than to every request at once.
action_items 2: Add an automatic guard that switches a recently changed io-shop flag back off when tail request latency rises after the change.
action_items 3: Require a cost-bounding test with large inputs, such as long purchase histories, for code behind a feature flag before that flag can be switched on in production.
action_items 4: Route the io-shop HighLatency alert to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
went_wrong 1: Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person was brought in while the incident ran.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged, and whether a went_wrong item is one its field excludes.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.

tools.name: judge_claims
